title: Tenali Raman and the Great Pundit of Kashi

full_text:
A renowned and arrogant scholar from Kashi named Vidyaranya Pandit arrived at the imperial court of Vijayanagara. He carried banners listing dozens of scholastic titles, escorted by disciples beating drums and announcing:
'Bow down before the invincible master of logic, grammar, and metaphysics! None in Bharatavarsha can stand before his philosophical debate!'

Vidyaranya challenged the court scholars of Vijayanagara to an open disputation on classical philosophy, demanding that if none dared face him, Emperor Krishnadevaraya must sign a proclamation acknowledging Kashi's intellectual supremacy and pay a tribute of ten thousand gold dinars.

The royal scholars of Vijayanagara, intimidated by the visitor's fierce reputation, lowered their heads and made excuses.
The King was mortified, fearing that the prestige of his illustrious empire would be permanently disgraced.

At the eleventh hour, Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, grant me permission to debate this scholar tomorrow morning. I shall defend the honor of Vijayanagara!'

The next morning, the grand audience hall was packed with courtiers, scholars, and foreign ambassadors.
Vidyaranya Pandit sat upon a raised silk dais, surrounded by stacks of ancient palm-leaf manuscripts.
Tenali Raman entered the hall with immense dignity, draped in the robes of a venerable grand master. In his hands, he carried a heavy bundle wrapped securely in fine crimson Benares silk and tied with a thick, coarse hemp rope.
He placed the bundle upon his desk with theatrical reverence.

Vidyaranya eyed the mysterious, imposing package with growing anxiety.
'Learned brother,' asked Vidyaranya cautiously, 'what sacred treatise is contained within that glorious silk wrapper? Upon which philosophical school shall we base our debate?'

Tenali stroked his chin and announced in a booming voice:
'This, revered Pandit, is the greatest philosophical masterpiece of our southern scholars: the immortal treatise entitled *Tilakashta Mahisha Bandhana*! We shall debate its third chapter on cosmic causality!'

Vidyaranya’s mind raced in frantic panic. *Tilakashta Mahisha Bandhana?*
He searched through forty years of memories of libraries in Kashi, Nalanda, and Mithila, but had never heard of such a text! He feared that if he confessed ignorance, his reputation as an all-knowing master would be shattered instantly.
Trembling, Vidyaranya requested a recess until the following morning to prepare his arguments.

That night, unable to find any reference to the mysterious treatise, Vidyaranya grew terrified of public humiliation. Under the cover of darkness, he packed his baggage and fled the city of Vijayanagara on his mule, leaving behind his banners and disciples!

At dawn, when the King found the challenger had fled, he turned to Tenali in amazed delight:
'Tenali, what divine, ancient book was inside that crimson silk bundle that terrified the great pundit into flight?'

Tenali laughed, unknotted the silk wrapper, and dumped its contents onto the King's table:
Inside was a small bundle of dry sesame stalks (*Tila-kashta*), tied to a rough hemp rope normally used to tether water buffaloes (*Mahisha-bandhana*)!

'Maharaj,' chuckled Tenali, 'it was merely firewood from sesame plants tied with a buffalo tether! The pretentious scholar was so blinded by his own complicated jargon that he fled from a handful of dry twigs and a rope!'

King Krishnadevaraya and the court roared with laughter, celebrating Tenali’s brilliant victory over pompous arrogance.
moral: Pretentious pedantry and inflated jargon collapse when challenged by quick wit and simple courage.

options: Wit and humor triumph over arrogance and power
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
